---
title: "Signals and plain objects"
subtitle: "Can a component hold reactive state without importing a framework — and why the kernel keeps signals at all"
---

Signals predate `provide()`. They arrived when a component was a class covered in
decorators, so "the component uses a Signal" and "the component imports the
reactive library" were the same sentence. Then components became plain objects,
and the question came back open: does reactive state drag the framework into a
class that had just been freed of it?

It does not, and this page is the demonstration — followed by the argument for
keeping signals, which is the part worth re-reading whenever the kernel looks
like it could be smaller.

## A plain class holds signals, with nothing declared

`reactive` is a service, so it arrives the way every other service arrives: as a
constructor argument named in `needs`.

```python
# services/timeouts.py — imports nothing, declares nothing, inherits nothing
class Timeouts:
    def __init__(self, reactive, seconds=30):
        self.seconds = reactive.signal(seconds)
        self._reactive = reactive

    def follow(self, client):
        self._reactive.effect(lambda: client.set_timeout(self.seconds.get()))
```

```python
# app.py — the only file that knows a kernel exists
from plugkit import ReactiveService, provide

await root.plugin(ReactiveService)
await root.plugin(
    provide(Timeouts, "timeouts", needs=["reactive"], config={"seconds": ("http.timeout", 30)})
)
```

No decorator, no base class, no annotation, no `plugkit` import in the component.
The class is testable with a two-line stand-in, because `reactive` is a parameter
rather than an ambient facility:

```python
import types
from plugkit import Effect, Signal

reactive = types.SimpleNamespace(signal=Signal, effect=Effect)
timeouts = Timeouts(reactive, seconds=5)
```

## The effects still die with the plugin

This is the part that would be easy to get wrong, and it works because of the
rebinding rule: reading a service through a context returns a view whose methods
are bound to the *reading* context. `provide()` reads `ctx.reactive` inside the
binding's own fiber, so the object the component stores on `self` is already
addressed to that fiber.

The consequence is stronger than it first looks. An effect the component
registers minutes later, from an ordinary method, is still owned by the fiber
that constructed the component — `follow()` above needs no lifetime plumbing.

Unload is total in both directions:

- effects registered in `__init__` and effects registered from a method both stop
  when the fiber unloads;
- registering after the fiber is gone does not leak, it raises —
  `CordisError: cannot create effect on inactive context`.

`test_binding.py::test_a_plain_component_registers_fiber_owned_effects` is that
property.

## The one thing a plain class cannot do

Create a *fiber-owned* effect having received nothing. This works, and is fully
plain:

```python
from plugkit.signals import Effect        # a standalone library, imports no kernel
```

but the `Effect` it makes belongs to whoever wrote the line, and the class must
dispose it in `close()`. That is not a gap to be closed. Ownership has to come
from somewhere, and the only honest way to get it is to be handed the owner — a
component that received nothing has nothing to attribute its registrations to.
Every alternative is an ambient registry, which is the leak this project exists
to delete.

So, three levels, all of them plain:

| what the class receives | what it can do | who disposes |
|---|---|---|
| nothing; `Signal` imported directly | hold reactive state | the class, in `close()` |
| `reactive` in its constructor | signals, computeds and effects | the fiber, automatically |
| nothing; `config={...}` on `provide()` | be rebuilt when a value changes | the fiber, automatically |

The third row is worth noticing: a component with no reactive awareness at all
still participates, because the binding watches the config keys its constructor
arguments came from and restarts the fiber when one changes.

## Why the kernel keeps signals

The vendored Cordis has exactly one notion of change: a fiber's epoch. Replace a
service *provider* and every dependent is torn down and re-applied. That is
correct when an object's identity changed — a dependent holding the old instance
holds a stale reference — and it is the wrong instrument for a value:

- **Granularity.** Reloading a plugin to observe a new timeout discards live
  connections, in-flight work and every other registration the plugin made, to
  propagate one integer. One Signal per config key wakes the readers of that key
  and nobody else.
- **The alternative is the leak.** Without signals, "tell me when this changes"
  becomes a callback list on some service — a subscription whose undo nobody
  holds. That is precisely the defect the whole kernel exists to make impossible,
  and it would arrive by the back door.
- **It makes the coarse mechanism usable.** `provide(config={...})` restarts a
  binding when the value behind a constructor argument changes. What tells it
  which bindings care is one Signal per key. Without that, the choice is polling
  or restarting everything.
- **It costs the kernel nothing.** `src/plugkit/signals.py` imports nothing from
  the kernel and `ReactiveService` is an ordinary plugin with no privileged
  status; a composition that never mounts it never pays for it — bindings still
  work, they just do not rebuild. Deleting the library would not shrink the
  kernel by a line. It would move the same work into every application, minus the
  ownership.

The two mechanisms are not rivals at different quality levels. They answer
different questions — *identity changed* versus *a value changed* — and each is
the wrong answer to the other one.
